newsitem.title: GERMANY: Trail goes cold for tsars' missing Amber Chamber.
newsitem.headline: Trail goes cold for tsars' missing Amber Chamber.

text.p: Hopes of finding the Amber Chamber, a tsarist treasure seized by the Nazis during World War Two, were dashed on Thursday when police said a newly-found fragment offered no clues to finding the rest.

Police in Potsdam said they were still sure a mosaic, traced to a notary's office in the port town of Bremen on Wednesday, was part of the elusive assembly of amber wall panels and furniture presented to the tsars by Prussia in 1712.

But they added that the small mosaic picture, depicting two couples relaxing in a garden landscape, had probably been separated from the rest of the chamber after the treasure was seized by Nazi troops during World War Two.

Police said told a news briefing that a German soldier had brought the mosaic back to Germany, while the rest of the chamber was being shipped to Kaliningrad, now a Russian enclave surrounded by Poland and Lithuania. Until 1945 the city was named Koenigsberg and was capital of East Prussia.
The soldier's son decided to approach a middleman last December to sell the mosaic, but German police said they caught him by posing as potential buyers.
The Amber Chamber was dismantled and removed from an imperial palace near St Petersburg, then Leningrad, by German troops in 1941.
It was last seen in Kaliningrad just before the German retreat in 1945. The chamber is at the top of Russia's list of missing treasures looted by the Nazis.

Last May, Bavarian police thought they were on the trail of the treasure when a hoax television film claiming that the chamber had being shipped across Germany was picked up as a top news story by two television stations.
Police rushed to intercept the shipment on a highway outside Munich, only to find the supposed artwork was a fake made for a TV spoof programme called "Can You Take a Joke?"
The treasure has been the object of frequent searches in Germany, with experts having combed cellars, caverns and lakes around Kaliningrad for decades searching for the panels.
